scenes.narration: One point six five trillion dollars. That is how much Americans owe on student loans, more than they owe on all their credit cards combined.

For five years, during and after the pandemic, most borrowers did not have to pay. Then missed payments came back on credit reports. In three months, the share of student debt at least ninety days late jumped from about half a percent to almost eight percent.
So who is actually in the business of America's student debt, and who ends up paying for it?

By the end of this video, you will know the four players in this business. The colleges that set the price, the government that lends the money, the companies that collect it, and the borrowers who fall behind.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with the price tag. According to the College Board, the average published tuition and fees at a public four-year college, for students from the same state, was about six thousand three hundred and twenty dollars in the school year that began in nineteen ninety-six, measured in today's dollars. This year, it is twelve thousand two hundred and ninety dollars. At private nonprofit colleges, it went from about twenty-seven thousand five hundred to forty-six thousand three hundred and fifty dollars. Those numbers are already adjusted for inflation.

The government's own price index tells the same story. By our calculation from Bureau of Labor Statistics data, the price of college tuition and fees rose about two hundred and fifty percent in the thirty years to September twenty twenty-six. Prices in general rose about one hundred and fourteen percent.

But there is a twist the headlines often miss. Over the last ten years, the inflation-adjusted sticker price at public four-year colleges actually fell by eight percent. And after grants and scholarships, the average net tuition paid by first-time, full-time in-state students there dropped from a peak of about four thousand six hundred dollars to an estimated one thousand nine hundred and twenty this year. The sticker price and the real price are not the same thing.

Still, most of the debt was already built up. Among students who finished a bachelor's degree in twenty twenty-five at public and private nonprofit four-year colleges, forty-seven percent graduated with debt, and the average borrower owed thirty thousand two hundred and twenty dollars.

Let me draw the gap. Here is the sticker price of a public college, almost doubling in thirty years after inflation. Here is what a typical student actually pays after grants, much lower. The space between those two lines is filled by grants, by family savings, and by loans. And for millions of students, the loan was the easiest piece to get.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Which brings us to the lender. And in America, the biggest student lender by far is not a bank.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: It is the federal government. The Federal Reserve's figures show Washington holding about one point six three trillion dollars of student loans, the vast majority of the total. The Education Department counts about forty-two million people who have federal student loans.

The pile grew fast. At the start of two thousand and three, Americans owed about two hundred and forty billion dollars in student loans, according to the New York Fed. Today it is one point six five trillion dollars. By our calculation, that is almost seven times as much in twenty-three years.

Was the government making money on all those loans? For years, its own estimates said yes. The Government Accountability Office looked at loans made from nineteen ninety-seven to twenty twenty-one. At first, the Education Department expected them to earn the government one hundred and fourteen billion dollars. Later estimates flipped that to a cost of one hundred and ninety-seven billion dollars. A swing of three hundred and eleven billion dollars.

The biggest single reason, about one hundred and two billion dollars of that swing, was the emergency relief of the pandemic, when payments and interest were paused. The rest came from changes in repayment plans and from estimates that turned out to be too optimistic about how much borrowers would repay.

Let me draw the government's balance. On one side, the interest it expected to collect. On the other, the money it lends and the payments it forgives or never gets back. When the loans were made, the scale tipped toward profit. Twenty years later, the same loans had tipped into a loss. The taxpayer ended up as the last link in the chain.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: But the government does not send the bills itself. For that, it hires private companies.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: They are called loan servicers. They send the statements, take the payments and answer the phone. According to the Government Accountability Office, in September twenty twenty-five the biggest of them, Nelnet, handled about five hundred and six billion dollars of loans for twelve point four million borrowers. Four other companies split most of the rest.

How do they get paid? Under the older contracts, the Education Department paid servicers a monthly fee for each borrower. About two dollars and eighty-five cents for a borrower in repayment. About a dollar for a student still in school. And only forty-five cents for a borrower more than two hundred and seventy days behind.

Think about what that pays for. A borrower in good standing was worth more to the servicer than one who fell far behind. Newer contracts from twenty twenty-four were meant to tie pay to performance, with penalties of up to twenty percent. But the government's own watchdog found that the agency overseeing them lost almost half its staff in twenty twenty-five, from one thousand four hundred and thirty-three people to seven hundred and seventy-seven.

And then there are the private lenders. Banks and other companies still lend to students, about about fifteen point four billion dollars in the last school year. That is far less than before the financial crisis, but it has been growing again for more than a decade.

Let me draw the chain. The student signs the loan. The government lends the money and owns the debt. A servicer sends the bills and is paid a fee. And the college receives the money at the very start, before anyone knows if the degree will pay off.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: For years, that chain was frozen. Then the pause ended.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: When missed payments returned to credit reports in early twenty twenty-five, the effect was immediate. The New York Fed found that more than two point two million borrowers who became newly delinquent saw their credit scores drop by more than one hundred points.
And it kept climbing. By the middle of twenty twenty-six, ten point six percent of all student loan balances were at least ninety days past due. Before the pause ended, it was close to zero.

Then came defaults. According to the New York Fed, roughly one million federal borrowers defaulted at the end of twenty twenty-five, and another two point six million in the first three months of twenty twenty-six. The Education Department's own data show defaulted Direct Loans more than doubling in a year, from eighty-two point six billion dollars to one hundred and eighty-seven point eight billion dollars.

Default is serious. The government can take part of a paycheck, a tax refund, even Social Security. Collections restarted in May twenty twenty-five, and were then put on hold. In May twenty twenty-six, the New York Fed noted they were suspended with no clear timeline for resumption.

Let me draw the cliff. Here is the share of student debt seriously late. For five years, a flat line near zero. Then, in a single quarter, a wall. Every point on that wall is a person whose credit score fell, whose car loan or apartment just became harder to get.

scenes.narration: Washington's answer was to change the rules of the whole business.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The plan that was supposed to make payments cheaper, called SAVE, was blocked in court. About eight million borrowers who had enrolled were placed in forbearance. On March tenth, twenty twenty-six, a federal court vacated the plan.

Meanwhile, Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed on July fourth, twenty twenty-five. It eliminated Grad PLUS loans for graduate students. New graduate students now face a limit of twenty thousand five hundred dollars a year and one hundred thousand dollars in total. Parents face new limits too. And a new Repayment Assistance Plan takes effect by July twenty twenty-six.

Let me put the business together. Colleges set the price. The government lends, and ended up carrying the losses. Servicers collect, paid by the borrower. And the borrowers carry the debt for decades. The new limits cap how much flows in at the top. Whether that pushes colleges to cut prices, or pushes students toward private lenders, is the question of the next decade.

So what is the business behind America's student debt? It was built on a simple promise. Borrow today, earn more tomorrow. For many graduates, that promise holds. But the bill has quietly been split between students, their parents, and taxpayers, while the money for the degree was paid on day one.
